### 2.5 Selected Integrals

By following the procedure outlined in the previous section, it is possible to cast all wavefunction coefficients of a conformally coupled scalar in a power-law FRW background as Euler-type twisted integrals of rational functions. In the following, we give some more complicated examples of such integrals, which will serve as useful test cases for the formalism developed in the rest of the paper. These integrals can be obtained systematically from the time-integral representation, but the integrand associated to a given graph is always the flat-space wavefunction coefficient, with the external energies shifted by integration variables, times a twist factor. Consequently, one can easily generate many examples by employing the combinatorial construction of the flat-space wavefunction in terms of graph tubings and then shifting the energies and integrating.

#### Three-site chain:

The next-simplest example is the wavefunction coefficient involving two exchanges. The exponential form of the bulk-to-boundary propagator for the conformally coupled scalar implies that the answer only depends on the total energy flowing out of a given vertex to the boundary, and so we suppress the external lines that connect to the boundary surface. The relevant graph is therefore the three-site chain

$$ X_{1} X_{2} X_{3} Y Y^{\prime} $$

where we have labeled the external energies by $X_{a}$ and the internal energies as $Y,Y^{\prime}$ . The wavefunction coefficient associated to this graph is

$$ \psi_{(3)}=\int_{0}^{\infty}(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3})^{\varepsilon}\,\Omega_{\psi}\,,\quad\text{where}\quad\Omega_{\psi}\equiv\frac{4YY^{\prime}}{B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}B_{4}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{5}}+\frac{1}{B_{6}}\right){\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\wedge{\rm d}x_{3}\,, $$

with the linear factors defined by

$$ \displaystyle B_{1} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+x_{1}+Y\,, \displaystyle\quad B_{4} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\,, \displaystyle B_{2} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+x_{2}+Y+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{5} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{3} \displaystyle\equiv X_{3}+x_{3}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{6} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+X_{3}+x_{2}+x_{3}+Y\,. $$

Comparing this integral to (2.15), we see that the integrand is exactly the flat-space wavefunction associated to this graph, written in dimensionless form and shifted by the integration variables.

#### Four-site chain:

We will also consider the four-site chain

$$ X_{1} X_{2} X_{3} X_{4} Y Y^{\prime} Y^{\prime\prime} $$

The associated wavefunction coefficient can be written as

$$ \psi_{(4)}^{(c)}=\int_{0}^{\infty}(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3}x_{4})^{\varepsilon}\,\Omega_{\psi}^{(c)}\,,\quad{\rm where}\quad\Omega_{\psi}^{(c)}\equiv\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}^{(c)}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\wedge{\rm d}x_{3}\wedge{\rm d}x_{4}\,\,. $$

The function in the integrand is the flat-space wavefunction for the four-site chain (with shifted arguments)

$$ \hat{\Omega}_{\psi}^{(c)}\equiv\psi_{\rm flat}^{(4,c)}(X_{a}+x_{a})=\frac{8YY^{\prime}Y^{\prime\prime}}{B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}B_{4}B_{5}}\left[\frac{1}{B_{6}B_{8}}+\frac{1}{B_{9}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{6}}+\frac{1}{B_{7}}\right)+\frac{1}{B_{10}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{7}}+\frac{1}{B_{8}}\right)\right], $$

where the linear factors are

$$ \displaystyle B_{1} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+x_{1}+Y\,, \displaystyle\quad B_{5} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}\,, \displaystyle B_{2} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+x_{2}+Y+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{6} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{3} \displaystyle\equiv X_{3}+x_{3}+Y^{\prime}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{7} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+X_{3}+x_{2}+x_{3}+Y+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{4} \displaystyle\equiv X_{4}+x_{4}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{8} \displaystyle\equiv X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{3}+x_{4}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{9} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{10} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}+Y\,. $$

The form of the function (2.31) is easily determined from the graph tubings described in Section 2.2.

#### Four-site star:

An interesting new phenomenon happens for graphs involving four sites (or three exchanges). In addition to the chain topology, we can also arrange the graph into a star by connecting three of the vertices to a single central vertex with valence three:

$$ X_{4} X_{3} X_{2} X_{1} Y^{\prime\prime} Y Y^{\prime} $$

The associated wavefunction coefficient takes the same form as (2.30), but the integrand is now

$$ \hat{\Omega}_{\psi}^{(s)}\equiv\ \frac{8YY^{\prime}Y^{\prime\prime}}{B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}B_{4}B_{5}}\bigg[\frac{1}{B_{9}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{6}}+\frac{1}{B_{7}}\right)\ +\frac{1}{B_{10}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{6}}+\frac{1}{B_{8}}\right)+\frac{1}{B_{11}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{7}}+\frac{1}{B_{8}}\right)\bigg]\,, $$

with

$$ \displaystyle B_{1} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+x_{1}+Y\,, \displaystyle\quad B_{5} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}\,, \displaystyle B_{2} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+x_{2}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{6} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{4}+x_{1}+x_{4}+Y^{\prime}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{3} \displaystyle\equiv X_{3}+x_{3}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{7} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+X_{4}+x_{2}+x_{4}+Y+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{4} \displaystyle\equiv X_{4}+x_{4}+Y+Y^{\prime}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{8} \displaystyle\equiv X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{3}+x_{4}+Y+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{9} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{4}+x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{4}+Y^{\prime\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{10} \displaystyle\equiv X_{1}+X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{1}+x_{3}+x_{4}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{11} \displaystyle\equiv X_{2}+X_{3}+X_{4}+x_{2}+x_{3}+x_{4}+Y\,, $$

The function (2.33)—the flat-space wavefunction coefficient for the four-site star $\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}^{(s)}\equiv\psi_{\rm flat}^{(4,s)}(X_{n}+x_{n})$ —is again easily derived from the graph tubings described in Section 2.2.

An important commonality of all the above integrals is that they are integrals of rational functions, whose singularities are associated to linear factors. The singularities of these integrals therefore lie along hyperplanes in the integration space; i.e. each integral is associated to a hyperplane arrangement. There is a rich mathematical theory of hyperplane arrangements (see Appendix A), which will aid us in developing the formalism to evaluate integrals of this type.

## 3 Case Study: Two-Site Chain

In the previous section, we showed that the wavefunction coefficients of a conformally coupled scalar in an FRW spacetime can be written as twisted integrals of the corresponding flat-space results. Specifically, for the two-site chain, we found

$$ \psi=-\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x_{1}{\rm d}x_{2}\,(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\frac{2Y}{(X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2})(X_{1}+x_{1}+Y)(X_{2}+x_{2}+Y)}\,. $$

Similar integrals arise for loop amplitudes in dimensional regularization. In that case, powerful mathematical tools have been used to evaluate these integrals, such as differential equations [73] and twisted cohomology [84]. We will now show that a similar approach is very effective for evaluating FRW correlators. In this section, we will present the analysis for the two-site chain as a case study,1010 10 While this work was being written up, related analyses of the two-site chain have appeared in [77, 85]. while, in the next section, we extend this to arbitrary tree graphs, bypassing many of the steps outlined here.

### 3.1 Differential Equation

The key idea is to enlarge the problem and consider a family of integrals with the same singularities as the original integral:

$$ I_{N}=\int(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\,\Omega_{N}\,,\quad\Omega_{N}\equiv\frac{{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}}{T_{1}^{m_{1}}T_{2}^{m_{2}}B_{1}^{n_{1}}B_{2}^{n_{2}}B_{3}^{n_{3}}}\,, $$

where $N\equiv(m_{1},m_{2},n_{1},n_{2},n_{3})$ is a set of integers and we have defined

$$ \displaystyle T_{1} \displaystyle\equiv x_{1}\,,\qquad\quad B_{1}\equiv X_{1}+x_{1}+Y\,, \displaystyle T_{2} \displaystyle\equiv x_{2}\,,\qquad\quad B_{2}\equiv X_{2}+x_{2}+Y\,,\qquad\quad B_{3}\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}\,. $$

The original integral (3.1) is one member of this family, namely $\psi=-2Y\times I_{00111}$ . Remarkably, the twisted integrals in (3.2) form a finite-dimensional vector space. This is not obvious from their definition, since the exponents $(m_{i},n_{i})$ have an infinite range. A finite basis of master integrals exists because all other integrals can be transformed into linear combinations of basis elements by a combination of partial fraction identities and integrations by parts, and so the integrals belong to equivalence classes. From a more abstract perspective, these equivalence classes are determined by the (twisted) cohomology induced by the exterior derivative (see Appendix A). Twisted cohomology also gives a simple way to predict the size of the vector space [86, 87]:

The number of independent master integrals is equal to the number of bounded regions defined by the divisors of the integrand.

Figure 2 shows the arrangement of the singular lines in the $(x_{1},x_{2})$ -plane. There are four bounded regions which implies that the vector space of integrals in (3.2) is four dimensional.

*Figure 2: Locations of the singular lines of the integrand in (3.1). We see that there are four bounded regions which implies a four-dimensional vector space of integrals in (3.2). The gray shaded region is associated to the original integral (3.1).*

It is convenient to collect the four independent master integrals into a four-component vector

$$ \vec{I}\equiv\left[\begin{array}[]{c}I_{1}\\
I_{2}\\
I_{3}\\
I_{4}\end{array}\right]=\int(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Omega_{1}\\
\Omega_{2}\\
\Omega_{3}\\
\Omega_{4}\end{array}\right], $$

where $\Omega_{a}$ are four independent two-forms. The existence of a finite-dimensional vector space has important consequences. In particular, it means that the master integrals must satisfy a set of coupled differential equations.

Consider taking derivatives with respect to the kinematic variables $Z_{I}\equiv\{X_{1},X_{2},Y\}$ . Whatever the result, it must be writable as a linear combination of the basis integrals. This leads to differential equations of the form

$$ \frac{\partial}{\partial Z_{I}}I_{a}=\sum_{b=1}^{4}A_{I,ab}I_{b}\,, $$

where the coefficients $A_{I,ab}$ are rational functions of the variables $Z_{I}$ . For each $I=1,2,3$ , we have a $4\times 4$ matrix $A_{I}$ with entries $A_{I,ab}$ . Defining the total differential ${\rm d}I_{a}\equiv\sum_{I}(\partial_{Z_{I}}I_{a})\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}Z_{I}$ and the matrix-valued one-form $A\equiv\sum_{I}A_{I}\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}Z_{I}$ , equation (3.5) can be written compactly as

$$ {\rm d}\vec{I}=A\,\vec{I}\,. $$

The form of $A$ will depend on our particular choice of basis, which we will discuss momentarily. Acting with ${\rm d}$ on (3.6) gives the constraint ${\rm d}A+A\wedge A=0$ .

A convenient choice of basis integrals is defined in terms of the canonical forms of the bounded regions (see box below). This choice is still not unique, since we have some freedom in choosing different bounded regions to tessellate the region in Figure 2. For all such choices, however, the differential equation (3.6) takes the so-called “ $\varepsilon$ -form” [72], where the right-hand side becomes proportional to the twist parameter:

$$ {\rm d}\vec{I}=\varepsilon\tilde{A}\,\vec{I}\,. $$

The fact that the source of this differential equation is linear in $\varepsilon$ has important consequences. First, a truncated Dyson series (or Chen iterated integral) gives a reliable approximation to the solution at small $\varepsilon$ (which is the case of interest for inflationary correlators). Moreover, the condition ${\rm d}A+A\wedge A=0$ becomes stronger for $\tilde{A}$ : it must separately satisfy ${\rm d}\tilde{A}=0$ and $\tilde{A}\wedge\tilde{A}=0$ , i.e. $\tilde{A}$ is an Abelian flat connection. The matrix $\tilde{A}$ can then be written as a sum of dlog forms

$$ \tilde{A}=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}\,{\rm d}\log\Phi_{i}(Z)\,, $$

where the functions $\Phi_{i}(Z)$ are the “letters” of the differential equation.

### 3.2 De Sitter Limit

*Figure 3: Illustration of the geometric meaning of the source functions arising in the differential equations for the de Sitter wavefunction.*

Before studying the most general form of the twisted integral (3.1), it is instructive to first consider the special case $\varepsilon=0$ . The corresponding untwisted integral gives the wavefunction in de Sitter space:

$$ \psi_{0}=\int\,\frac{-2Y}{B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\equiv\int\Omega_{\psi}\,, $$

where $\Omega_{\psi}\equiv\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}$ is the canonical form of the triangle bounded by $\{B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}\}=0$ .

Importantly, the integrand in (3.11) depends only on the combinations $X_{1}+x_{1}$ and $X_{2}+x_{2}$ . When we take a derivative with respect to the external energy $X_{1}$ , we therefore have $\partial_{X_{1}}\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}=\partial_{x_{1}}\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}$ , so that we get a total derivative in the integration variable $x_{1}$ . Evaluating this integral on its boundary, we find

$$ \partial_{X_{1}}\psi_{0}=\int{\rm d}x_{2}\,(-\hat{\Omega}_{\psi})\Big|_{x_{1}=0}=f(X_{1})\int{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{B_{2}}{B_{3}}\right)\bigg|_{x_{1}=0}\equiv f(X_{1})F_{0}\,, $$

where we have written the result in terms of the unique one-form on the line $x_{1}=0$ that shares a nontrivial residue with $(-\hat{\Omega}_{\psi})\big|_{x_{1}=0}$ , i.e. the form associated to the red interval in Figure 3. Matching residues at $(x_{1}=0,B_{2}=0)$ on both sides of (3.12) gives $f(X_{1})=2Y/(X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2})$ , so that

$$ \partial_{X_{1}}\psi_{0}=\left(\frac{1}{X_{1}-Y}-\frac{1}{X_{1}+Y}\right)F_{0}\,. $$

Similarly, taking derivatives with respect to $X_{2}$ and $Y$ gives

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{X_{2}}\psi_{0} \displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{X_{2}-Y}-\frac{1}{X_{2}+Y}\right)\tilde{F}_{0}\,, \displaystyle\partial_{Y}\psi_{0} \displaystyle=-\left(\frac{1}{X_{1}-Y}+\frac{1}{X_{1}+Y}\right)F_{0}-\left(\frac{1}{X_{2}-Y}+\frac{1}{X_{2}+Y}\right)\tilde{F}_{0}\,, $$

where $\tilde{F}_{0}$ is associated to the canonical form of the blue interval on $x_{2}=0$ in Figure 3.

Next, we take derivatives of the source functions $F_{0}$ and $\tilde{F}_{0}$ . Starting from the definition of $F_{0}$ in (3.12), its $X_{1}$ -derivative is

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}F_{0}=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x_{2}\,\partial_{x_{2}}\left(-\frac{1}{B_{3}}\right)\bigg|_{x_{1}=0}=\frac{1}{B_{3}}\bigg|_{x_{1}=x_{2}=0} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}} \displaystyle\equiv\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\,Z_{0}\,, $$

where we have defined the “function” $Z_{0}\equiv 1$ for later convenience. Similarly, for the $X_{2}$ -derivative, we get

$$ \displaystyle\hskip 28.45274pt\partial_{X_{2}}F_{0}=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x_{2}\,\partial_{x_{2}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{2}}-\frac{1}{B_{3}}\right)\bigg|_{x_{1}=0} \displaystyle=-\left(\frac{1}{B_{2}}-\frac{1}{B_{3}}\right)\bigg|_{x_{1}=x_{2}=0} \displaystyle\equiv\left(-\frac{1}{X_{2}+Y}+\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\right)\,Z_{0}\,. $$

Finally, the $Y$ -derivative gives

$$ \partial_{Y}F_{0}=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x_{2}\,\partial_{x_{2}}\frac{1}{B_{2}}=-\frac{1}{X_{2}+Y}Z_{0}\,. $$

By permutation symmetry, $\partial_{X_{1}}\tilde{F}_{0}$ and $\partial_{X_{2}}\tilde{F}_{0}$ satisfy the same equations with $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ interchanged, while $\partial_{Y}\tilde{F}_{0}$ is equal to $\partial_{Y}F_{0}$ with $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ interchanged.

Defining the total differential, ${\rm d}\equiv\sum_{I}\partial_{Z_{I}}{\rm d}Z_{I}$ (where $Z_{I}$ includes both the external energies $X_{1,2}$ and the exchange energy $Y$ ), we can combine these equations as

In this system of equations, taking a differential produces “simpler” functions, which is a characteristic of polylogarithmic functions. The information encoded in (3.18) can also be repackaged using the symbol of a transcendental function (for details, see Appendix E). The symbol $\cal S$ of a function $F^{(n)}$ of transcendental weight $n$ is defined recursively by the relation

$$ {\rm d}F^{(n)}=\sum_{i}F_{i}^{(n-1)}\,{\rm d}\log R_{i}\quad\Rightarrow\quad{\cal S}(F^{(n)})\equiv\sum_{i}{\cal S}(F_{i}^{(n-1)})\otimes R_{i}\,, $$

where $R_{i}$ are rational functions of the variables associated to the differential. This is consistent with the structure of the differential equations (3.18), with $R_{i}$ involving ratios of the letters $\Phi_{j}/\Phi_{l}$ . From this definition, we see that the symbol of the de Sitter wavefunction is

$$ {\cal S}(\psi_{0})=\frac{X_{1}+X_{2}}{X_{2}+Y}\otimes\frac{X_{1}-Y}{X_{1}+Y}+\frac{X_{1}+X_{2}}{X_{1}+Y}\otimes\frac{X_{2}-Y}{X_{2}+Y}\,. $$

The symbol can also be determined by other recursive methods, using either bulk perturbation theory [7] or cosmological polytopes [4]. It is interesting that the same building blocks that appear in the symbol here arise in the differential equations satisfied by the master integrals. This is highly nontrivial, and a more detailed discussion can be found in Appendix E.

### 3.3 FRW Integral

*Figure 4: Illustration of the geometry behind the functions defined in this section. Associated to each bounded region is a two-form. Each triangle contains one vertex that isn’t shared with any other triangle, so any two-form can be decomposed into this basis by matching residues at these special points.*

After this warmup in de Sitter space, we now consider the twisted case:

$$ \psi=\int\,(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\,\Omega_{\psi}\,. $$

We define a specific integral basis in terms of the canonical forms associated to the four shaded triangles in Figure 4.1111 11 The selection of these boundary regions is of course not unique, and in principle any four linearly independent combinations of the canonical forms in (3.22) can function as a basis. Alternative choices of the basis yield different matrix forms, with varied coefficients and levels of sparsity, etc. Nevertheless, as we will elucidate in later sections, this specific integral basis possesses a canonical character, enabling the reinterpretation of the corresponding differential equations in combinatorial terms. Using (3.10), we have

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\psi} \displaystyle={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{B_{1}}{B_{3}}\right)\wedge{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{B_{2}}{B_{3}}\right)=\frac{-2Y}{B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{F} \displaystyle={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{T_{1}}{B_{3}}\right)\wedge{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{B_{2}}{B_{3}}\right)=\frac{X_{1}-Y}{T_{1}B_{2}B_{3}}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{F}} \displaystyle={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{B_{1}}{B_{3}}\right)\wedge{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{T_{2}}{B_{3}}\right)=\frac{X_{2}-Y}{B_{1}T_{2}B_{3}}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{Z} \displaystyle={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{T_{1}}{B_{3}}\right)\wedge{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{T_{2}}{B_{3}}\right)=\frac{X_{1}+X_{2}}{T_{1}T_{2}B_{3}}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\,. $$

Given this choice of bounded regions and associated canonical forms, the basis of integrals is

$$ \vec{I}\equiv\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\psi\\
F\\
\tilde{F}\\
Z\end{array}\right]=\int(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Omega_{\psi}\\
\Omega_{F}\\
\Omega_{\tilde{F}}\\
\Omega_{Z}\end{array}\right]. $$

To derive the differential equation, we take derivatives of these basis integrals with respect to the external energies. As before, we have $\partial_{X_{1}}\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}=\partial_{x_{1}}\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}$ . This time, however, integration by parts will pick up a contribution from the twist factor:

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{X_{1}}\psi=\int(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\,\partial_{x_{1}}\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\int(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\,\left(-\frac{1}{T_{1}}\,\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}\right){\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\int(x_{1}x_{2})^{\varepsilon}\,\left(g(X_{1})\,\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}+f(X_{1})\,\hat{\Omega}_{F}\right){\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}\,, $$

where, in the second line, we have expanded the result into the basis of two-forms. The only two-forms that share nontrivial residues with the integrand $(-\hat{\Omega}_{\psi}/T_{1})$ , are those associated to the gray and red triangles in Figure 4. Matching residues at $(B_{1}=0,B_{2}=0)$ and $(T_{1}=0,B_{2}=0)$ , respectively, we find $g(X_{1})=1/(X_{1}+Y)$ and $f(X_{1})=2Y/(X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2})$ , so that

$$ \partial_{X_{1}}\psi=\frac{\varepsilon}{X_{1}+Y}(\psi-F)+\frac{\varepsilon}{X_{1}-Y}F\,. $$

By symmetry, $\partial_{X_{2}}\psi$ gives the same equation with $X_{1}\to X_{2}$ and $F\to\tilde{F}$ . Finally, since $Y$ appears only as $X_{1,2}\pm Y$ , the $\partial_{Y}$ equations don’t produce any new functions, like in the untwisted case.

The rest of the calculation then proceeds in the same way. We take derivatives of the source functions and expand the result in terms of the basis functions, where the coefficient functions are determined by matching residues. This leads to the following total differentials

All integrals have weight $2\varepsilon$ under rescalings of the energies $Z_{I}\equiv\{X_{1},X_{2},Y\}$ . In other words, the dilation operator acts as

$$ \sum_{I}Z_{I}\frac{\partial}{\partial Z_{I}}\ \vec{I}=2\varepsilon\,\vec{I}\,. $$

An important consequence of this constraint is that the sum of all coefficients in each differential equals $2\varepsilon$ times the parent function: all source functions cancel in pairs. For example, for the wavefunction $\psi$ , we have

$$ \sum_{I}Z_{I}\frac{\partial}{\partial Z_{I}}\psi=\varepsilon\,\big[(\psi-F)+F+(\psi-\tilde{F})+\tilde{F}\big]=2\varepsilon\,\psi\,, $$

where the sum indeed involves all coefficients of the dlog forms appearing in ${\rm d}\psi$ .

Before considering the solution of (3.26), let us show that these equations become the correct de Sitter equations (3.18) in the limit $\varepsilon\to 0$ . Before taking this limit, we define $Z^{\prime}\equiv\varepsilon^{2}Z$ , $F^{\prime}\equiv\varepsilon F$ , $\tilde{F}^{\prime}\equiv\varepsilon\tilde{F}$ , so that

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\psi \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\big]\,\psi \displaystyle+\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)-{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\big]\hskip 1.0ptF^{\prime}+\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)-{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\big]\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{F}^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}F^{\prime} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\big]\hskip 1.0ptF^{\prime}+\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})-{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\big]\hskip 1.0ptZ^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\tilde{F}^{\prime} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)+{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\big]\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{F}^{\prime}+\big[{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})-{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\big]\hskip 1.0ptZ^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}Z^{\prime} \displaystyle=2\varepsilon\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\hskip 1.0ptZ^{\prime}\,. $$

Sending $\varepsilon\to 0$ then amounts to deleting the diagonal entries of the matrix, reproducing (3.18).

The above system of differential equations can be recast as a matrix differential equation, ${\rm d}\vec{I}=\varepsilon\tilde{A}\,\vec{I}$ , with $\tilde{A}$ taking the form

$$ \tilde{A}=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}\phantom{\hskip 3.0pt}\ell_{1}+\ell_{2}&\phantom{\hskip 3.0pt}\ell_{3}-\ell_{1}&\phantom{\hskip 3.0pt}\ell_{4}-\ell_{2}&0\\[5.0pt]
0&\ell_{2}+\ell_{3}&0&\ell_{5}-\ell_{2}\\[5.0pt]
0&0&\ell_{1}+\ell_{4}&\phantom{\hskip 3.0pt}\ell_{5}-\ell_{1}\\[5.0pt]
0&0&0&2\ell_{5}\end{array}\right], $$

where we have defined

$$ \displaystyle\ell_{1} \displaystyle\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\,,\qquad\ell_{3}\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)\,, \displaystyle\ell_{2} \displaystyle\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,,\qquad\ell_{4}\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\,,\qquad\ell_{5}\equiv{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,. $$

It can be readily checked that the integrability condition is satisfied, $\tilde{A}\wedge\tilde{A}=0$ ,1212 12 In order to check this equation, we use $\ell_{1,2}\wedge\ell_{4,3}+\ell_{4,3}\wedge\ell_{5}+\ell_{5}\wedge\ell_{1,2}=0$ , which follows from $(X_{1}\pm Y)+(X_{2}\mp Y)=X_{1}+X_{2}$ . This will be important later to show consistency of $\tilde{A}$ for more complicated diagrams. while ${\rm d}\tilde{A}=0$ is trivially satisfied because the matrix is given by a sum of exact forms with constant coefficients. We also see that the matrix is upper triangular. The matrix differential equation is therefore amenable to an iterative solution, ascending through rows, each time solving a first-order equation, and then using the solution as a source in the subsequent row’s equation. Interestingly, $\tilde{A}$ has “folded singularities” as $X_{1,2}\to Y$ , which are singularities that arise when two (or more) momenta become collinear. These singularities shouldn’t exist in physical correlation functions (for the usual adiabatic vacuum initial conditions), and enforcing the absence of these singularities in the solutions is an important boundary condition (see below).

#### Explicit solution:

With the matrix $\tilde{A}$ in hand, let us now solve the system of differential equations. The easiest entries are $Z$ and the linear combination $\psi_{D}\equiv\psi-F-\tilde{F}+Z$ :1313 13 This combination doesn’t have a singularity in the total energy, hence the subscript $D$ for “disconnected.” Explicitly, the integral is

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}Z \displaystyle=2\varepsilon\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,Z\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\psi_{D} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\Big[{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\Big]\,\psi_{D}\,. $$

It is easy show that the solutions to these equations are

The normalizations of these solutions can be fixed by performing the integrals explicitly for specific kinematics (or by imposing appropriate boundary conditions on the full solution; see Appendix D). Evaluating $Z$ for $X_{1}=X_{2}=1/2$ and $\psi_{D}$ for $X_{1}=X_{2}=0$ , $Y=1$ gives

where ${}_{2}F_{1}$ is the Gauss hypergeometric function. The normalization of the solution can again be fixed by performing the integral for specific kinematics. Evaluating $F$ for $X_{1}=X_{2}=0$ yields

A similar analysis for $\tilde{F}$ leads to the same result with $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ interchanged. By shifting the indices of the hypergeometric function, we can absorb the terms proportional to $c_{F}$ .

Even though the original energy integral in (3.1) only converged for $\varepsilon>-1$ , this solution to the differential equations contains the physical wavefunctions for any $\varepsilon$ . The result (3.42) is a meromorphic function of $\varepsilon$ with poles at integer and positive half-integer values of $\varepsilon$ , as can be seen from the normalization factors in (3.37). ### 3.4 Cosmology-Shift Relations

For the two-site process, we have the explicit solution (3.42) for any value of $\varepsilon$ , but we will not have this luxury for more complicated correlation functions. It turns out that knowing the wavefunction at a particular value of $\varepsilon$ gives us a way to obtain it for other cosmologies that differ in $\varepsilon$ by integer units. This is due to shift relations between the integrals. Similar shift relations are standard in scattering amplitudes, where a shift in $\varepsilon$ relates the amplitudes computed in different spacetime dimensions.

The proof of the existence of shift relations is simple: a shift in $\varepsilon$ of all master integrals is just a change of basis in the same vector space. Hence, they must be related by a rotation matrix:

$$ \vec{I}(\varepsilon-1)=M(Z,\varepsilon)\,\vec{I}(\varepsilon)\,, $$

where $M$ satisfies ${\rm d}M+\tilde{A}M=\varepsilon[\tilde{A},M]$ and is invertible for $\varepsilon\neq\tfrac{1}{2},1$ . If one insists on relating directly the wavefunctions, instead of the whole basis, that is also possible. We simply use the flat connection $A$ to write the other basis members in terms of derivatives of the wavefunction. In that case, the cosmology-shift relation is performed by a differential operator.1414 14 In fact, the origin of such cosmology-shifting differential operators is easy to see from the time integral representation. For cubic interactions, lowering $\varepsilon$ by one unit amounts to introducing an extra factor of $\eta_{i}$ for each vertex $i$ . This is easily achieved with the differential operator $D_{-}=\prod_{i}\partial_{X_{i}}$ , which acts on the product of the bulk-to-boundary propagators $\prod_{i}e^{iX_{i}\eta_{i}}$ and effectively shifts $\varepsilon$ . Similar differential operators that shift the masses of scalar fields were studied in flat space [88] and de Sitter space [32, 33].

The matrix $M$ can be found using partial fractions and integrations by part. We obtain

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{\varepsilon-1}=\frac{1}{(X_{1}+Y)(X_{2}+Y)}\left(\psi_{\varepsilon}+\frac{2Y}{X_{1}-1}F_{\varepsilon}+\frac{2Y}{X_{2}-1}\tilde{F}_{\varepsilon}-\frac{2Y}{X_{1}+X_{2}}Z_{\varepsilon}\right), \displaystyle\begin{split}F_{\varepsilon-1}&=\frac{1}{(X_{1}-Y)(X_{2}+Y)}\,F_{\varepsilon}+\left(\frac{1-2\varepsilon}{(1-\varepsilon)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(X_{2}+Y)(X_{1}+X_{2})}\right)Z_{\varepsilon}\,,\\
\tilde{F}_{\varepsilon-1}&=\frac{1}{(X_{1}+Y)(X_{2}-Y)}\,\tilde{F}_{\varepsilon}+\left(\frac{1-2\varepsilon}{(1-\varepsilon)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{2}}-\frac{1}{(X_{1}+Y)(X_{1}+X_{2})}\right)Z_{\varepsilon}\,,\\
\end{split} \displaystyle Z_{\varepsilon-1}=\frac{2(1-2\varepsilon)}{(1-\varepsilon)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{2}}\,Z_{\varepsilon}\,. $$

We see that the shift relation is algebraic, and hence care must be taken when using it at certain (half-)integer values of $\varepsilon$ . For example, in the de Sitter limit $\varepsilon\to 0$ , only $\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}Z_{\varepsilon}=1/\varepsilon^{2}$ survives on the right-hand side. Keeping only $Z_{\varepsilon}$ , we see that the shift relation gives the correct expression for the flat-space wavefunction $\psi_{-1}$ in terms of the basis functions for $\varepsilon=0$ , despite the fact that the de Sitter wavefunction is a transcendental function. On the other hand, the relation is invalid for $\varepsilon=\frac{1}{2},1$ because the basis functions on the right-hand side are rational functions, while the wavefunctions for $\varepsilon=-\frac{1}{2},0$ are transcendental functions.

### 3.5 Locality and Time Evolution

The wavefunction $\psi$ , and more generally the family of twisted integrals we have encountered, is rather special from a mathematical perspective. This is maybe not too surprising, because we expect that objects with a physical interpretation have a somewhat distinguished status in the space of all possible mathematical objects with similar properties. One obvious special feature of the integral family (3.2) is that only two out of the five singular lines are twisted. This seemingly innocuous fact has a dramatic consequence: the physical wavefunction of interest satisfies a local differential equation. As we will see, this is a non-generic situation, and more generic twists do not lead to local differential equations.

#### Local evolution:

Since the integral basis is four dimensional, each member of the basis will satisfy at most a fourth-order ordinary homogeneous differential equation in each of $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ . A small surprise is that we instead get a third-order equation. Explicitly, the wavefunction satisfies

$$ \displaystyle\Big[(X_{1}+X_{2})(X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2})\,\partial^{3}_{X_{1}} \displaystyle-\big[(1-2\varepsilon)Y^{2}-2X_{1}X_{2}(2-\varepsilon)-X_{1}^{2}(5-4\varepsilon)\big]\,\partial^{2}_{X_{1}} \displaystyle+(1-\varepsilon)\big(X_{1}(4-5\varepsilon)+X_{2}(2-\varepsilon)\big)\,\partial_{X_{1}}-\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)(1-2\varepsilon)\Big]\,\psi=0\,, $$

and, by symmetry, an equivalent equation holds in $X_{2}$ .

Note that the coefficients in (3.45) depend on both $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ , so that the equation looks “non-local,” in the sense that it seems to depend on the energies of both interaction vertices from the bulk perspective. However, the equation can also be written as

$$ \partial_{X_{1}}\Big[(X_{1}+X_{2})^{1-2\varepsilon}\big((X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2})\partial_{X_{1}}^{2}+2(1-\varepsilon)X_{1}\partial_{X_{1}}-\varepsilon(1-\varepsilon)\big)\Big]\,\psi=0\,, $$

which can then be integrated to give a local, inhomogeneous second-order equation1515 15 In the mathematical literature, equations like (3.46) are also referred to as Picard–Fuchs equations; moreover, the differential operator annihilating the wavefunction function in (3.45) is called the Picard–Fuchs operator. There are interesting algorithms to derive the Picard–Fuchs equations directly without going through the procedure described in this paper [89, 90, 91].

where $g$ is a constant of integration. A simple way to arrive at the same result is by solving (3.26) iteratively. Integrating the equation for $Z$ is trivial and leads to $Z=c_{Z}(X_{1}+X_{2})^{2\varepsilon}$ . The remaining equations can then be written as

$$ \displaystyle\frac{X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2}}{2}\left(\partial_{X_{1}}-\frac{\varepsilon}{X_{1}+Y}\right)\psi \displaystyle=\varepsilon F\,, \displaystyle\left(\partial_{X_{1}}-\frac{\varepsilon}{X_{1}-Y}\right)F \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,c_{Z}\,\left(\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\right)^{1-2\varepsilon}\,, $$

which can easily be combined into the form (3.47).

Importantly, the differential operator on the left-hand side of (3.47) depends only on $X_{1}$ (and not on $X_{2}$ ). This reflects the fact that the wavefunction comes from local evolution in the bulk spacetime. To see this, we start from the bulk time integral (2.25):

$$ \psi\propto\int{\rm d}\eta\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\eta^{\prime}\,(\eta\eta^{\prime})^{-(1+\varepsilon)}\,e^{iX_{1}\eta}\,G(Y;\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,e^{iX_{2}\eta^{\prime}}\,, $$

where the bulk-to-bulk propagator satisfies

$$ \big(\partial_{\eta}^{2}+Y^{2}\big)G(Y;\eta,\eta^{\prime})=-i\delta(\eta-\eta^{\prime})\,. $$

The fact that $G$ obeys this differential equation can be used to derive a differential equation for the function $\psi$ . We simply consider the auxiliary object

$$ F\equiv\int{\rm d}\eta\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\eta^{\prime}\,(\eta\eta^{\prime})^{-(1+\varepsilon)}\,e^{iX_{1}\eta}e^{iX_{2}\eta^{\prime}}\,\eta^{2}\big(\partial_{\eta}^{2}+Y^{2}\big)G(Y;\eta,\eta^{\prime})\,, $$

and evaluate it in two different ways. First, we use (3.51) to compute the integral directly. The delta function $\delta(\eta-\eta^{\prime})$ reduces this to a one-dimensional time integral leading to the contact term on the right-hand side of (3.47). Second, we integrate the time derivatives in (3.52) by parts and trade factors of $\eta$ for $-i\partial_{X_{1}}$ . Pulling the energy derivatives outside of the time integrals produces the left-hand side of (3.47). This illustrates how the inhomogeneous second-order equation (3.47) reflects local evolution in the bulk spacetime. In some sense, we can think of the existence of a local differential operator that simplifies the singularity structure of $\psi$ as a reflection of its origin from local spacetime physics.

#### When is it local?

We found that the integral $\psi$ obeys two separate second-order inhomogeneous differential equations in each variable $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ . This is a simpler state of affairs than we could have hoped for, since a generic arrangement of five hyperplanes and twists yields a fourth-order homogeneous differential equation with coefficients depending on both $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ . Of course, the reason for this simplification is that our integral comes from a local spacetime process mediated by the exchange of a particle with a two-derivative equation of motion. However, more abstractly, we can ask what mathematical property of the arrangement of hyperplanes and twists gives rise to a pair of local differential equations. In other words, if we were given a random set of exponents and hyperplanes, how could we determine whether the resulting integral describes local evolution in spacetime? This is a deep question, for which we do not have a complete answer, but in the following we explore it in the context of our specific problem.

Let us consider the most general twisting of the hyperplane arrangement depicted in Figure 2, with five twist parameters $\varepsilon_{i}$ . The relevant integral family then is

$$ I_{N}\equiv\int{\rm d}x_{1}{\rm d}x_{2}\,\frac{1}{T_{1}^{m_{1}-\varepsilon_{1}}T_{2}^{m_{2}-\varepsilon_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}B_{1}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}n_{1}+\varepsilon_{3}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}B_{2}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}n_{2}+\varepsilon_{4}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}B_{3}^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}n_{3}+\varepsilon_{5}}}}}\,, $$

which again only has four basis elements. We take the basis to be defined by the same canonical forms as before. The first-order differential equation obeyed by this basis then again takes the form ${\rm d}\vec{I}=A\,\vec{I}$ , with

$$ \hskip-7.0ptA=\left[\begin{array}[]{cccc}\varepsilon_{1}\ell_{1}+\varepsilon_{2}\ell_{2}-\varepsilon_{345}^{+}\ell_{6}&\varepsilon_{1}(\ell_{3}-\ell_{1})&\varepsilon_{2}(\ell_{4}-\ell_{2})&0\\[5.0pt]
\varepsilon_{3}(\ell_{1}-\ell_{6})&\varepsilon_{2}\ell_{2}-\varepsilon_{3}\ell_{1}-\varepsilon_{451}^{-}\ell_{3}&0&\varepsilon_{2}(\ell_{5}-\ell_{2})\\[5.0pt]
\varepsilon_{4}(\ell_{2}-\ell_{6})&0&\varepsilon_{1}\ell_{1}-\varepsilon_{4}\ell_{2}-\varepsilon_{352}^{-}\ell_{4}&\varepsilon_{1}(\ell_{5}-\ell_{1})\\[5.0pt]
0&\varepsilon_{4}(\ell_{2}-\ell_{3})&\varepsilon_{3}(\ell_{1}-\ell_{4})&\varepsilon_{125}^{-}\ell_{5}-\varepsilon_{3}\ell_{1}-\varepsilon_{4}\ell_{2}\end{array}\right]\!, $$

where $\varepsilon_{ijk}^{\pm}\equiv\varepsilon_{i}+\varepsilon_{j}\pm\varepsilon_{k}$ and $\ell_{i}$ denote the forms defined in (3.31), with the new letter $\ell_{6}\equiv{\rm d}\log Y$ . Notice that it reduces to $\varepsilon\tilde{A}$ for $\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{2}=\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon_{3}=\varepsilon_{4}=\varepsilon_{5}=0$ . As expected, the matrix is linear in the twists, and the coefficients of each twist parameter are $\pm 1$ .

First, we discuss the case with distinct twists $\varepsilon_{1}\neq\varepsilon_{2}$ on $x_{1}$ and $x_{2}$ , and no twists on the other lines, $\varepsilon_{3}=\varepsilon_{4}=\varepsilon_{5}=0$ . The most notable features of the special case $\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{2}\equiv\varepsilon$ are preserved: the matrix $A$ is still triangular and leads to a third-order homogeneous differential equation (one order lower than expected in the generic case). Furthermore, this homogeneous differential equation still implies a local second-order equation, which now takes the form

$$ \Delta_{X_{1}}^{(\varepsilon_{1})}\psi=g^{2}\left(\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\right)^{1-(\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{2})}\,, $$

where $\Delta_{X_{1}}^{(\varepsilon_{1})}\equiv(X_{1}^{2}-Y^{2})\partial_{X_{1}}^{2}+2(1-\varepsilon_{1})X_{1}\partial_{X_{1}}-\varepsilon_{1}(1-\varepsilon_{1})$ is the same operator as in (3.47). It is not surprising that $\varepsilon_{1}\neq\varepsilon_{2}$ still leads to a local equation, since we could implement this form of twisting by having two different cubic couplings with some relative time dependence in the bulk spacetime. Hence, there is still a natural bulk spacetime interpretation of these objects.

Next, we explore under which conditions twisting of the lines $\{B_{1},B_{2},B_{3}\}$ leads to local equations. We first impose that each basis integral satisfies a third-order homogeneous differential equation (and not a fourth-order equation). We find that this requires $\varepsilon_{3}=\varepsilon_{4}=0$ ; i.e. any twisting of the lines associated to the partial energy singularities would lead to non-locality. On the other hand, a twisting of the total energy line, $\varepsilon_{5}\neq 0$ , is allowed and leads to

$$ \bigg(\Delta_{X_{1}}^{(\varepsilon_{1})}+\varepsilon_{5}\Big[(Y+X_{1})\partial_{X_{1}}-\varepsilon_{1}\Big]\bigg)\,\psi\ =\ g^{2}\left(\frac{1}{X_{1}+X_{2}}\right)^{1-(\varepsilon_{1}+\varepsilon_{2}-\varepsilon_{5})}\,. $$

In this case, there is indeed a two-derivative operator collapsing the exchange diagram to a contact solution. However, this operator is qualitatively different from the previous case. The single-derivative term, proportional to $\varepsilon_{5}$ , has a different weight in $X_{1}$ and does not amount to a mere redefinition of the scalar coefficients appearing in the second-order equation (3.47). The spacetime interpretation is a term linear in $\eta$ in the equation of motion for the bulk-to-bulk propagator:

$$ \left(\partial_{\eta}^{2}+\frac{\varepsilon_{5}}{\eta}(iY-\partial_{\eta})+Y^{2}\right)G(Y;\eta,\eta^{\prime})=-i\delta(\eta-\eta^{\prime})\,. $$

In flat space, this modified propagator gives the wavefunction

$$ \displaystyle\psi_{\rm flat}=\frac{1}{(X_{1}+Y)(X_{2}+Y)(X_{1}+X_{2})^{1+\varepsilon_{5}}}\,, $$

consistent with (3.53). It can readily be checked that this satisfies (3.56) for $\varepsilon_{1}=\varepsilon_{2}=-1$ . However, it is evident that the term linear in $Y$ in (3.57) is spatially non-local (recall that $Y\equiv|\vec{k}_{1}+\vec{k}_{2}|$ , so this is non-analytic in $\vec{k}_{1,2}$ ). Thus, only the twisting of the coordinate planes corresponds to the physical wavefunction arising from a local process in the bulk spacetime.

## 4 An Algorithm for All Trees

In the previous section, we studied in detail the differential equations for the two-site chain, where the integrals were two-dimensional and their singularities could easily be visualized as lines in the plane. We will also be interested, however, in more complicated graphs like

$$  $$

In those cases, the integrals are higher-dimensional and therefore much harder to visualize. To analyze such examples, we need a more algebraic approach.

In this section, we will introduce a general algorithm to derive the differential equations for arbitrary tree graphs. Although this approach will be completely systematic, for sufficiently complicated graphs it can become rather tedious and the results often aren’t very illuminating. However, a closer inspection of the differential equations reveals something remarkable. As we will show in Section 5, the structure of the differential equations obeys very simple graphical rules, which will allow us to understand the differential equations for all tree graphs. Readers who don’t want to be distracted by technical aspects are therefore invited to skip this section and look directly at the efficient graphical representation of the results in Section 5.

The algorithm has two essential features. For an $n$ -dimensional integral, we first enumerate a basis of integrals by considering all possible projective simplices involving $n$ planes, along with the plane at infinity. We then construct linear combinations that are boundary-less (in an appropriately defined sense), so that they correspond to bounded regions. The canonical forms of these regions then provide a specific basis of master integrals. The derivatives of the canonical forms associated to the simplices, with respect to external data, can be written as a linear combination of the basis of simplices—cf. (4.11). It is then a matter of algebra to take derivatives of a given integral and decompose the result into the chosen basis. In this section, we will describe the detailed implementation of this strategy for the two- and three-site graphs, but the approach is sufficiently algorithmic that it can easily be implemented for arbitrary graphs, and we discuss some features of these more complicated situations. Further examples are presented in a Mathematica notebook, which is available at a github repository for this paper .

### 4.1 A Simplex Basis

We have seen that the FRW wavefunction associated to a general graph can be written as a twisted integral of a rational function. At tree level, the wavefunction arising from a graph with $n-1$ exchanges can be written as an $n$ -dimensional integral, and the singularities of the integrand define a hyperplane arrangement in ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ . Denoting these hyperplanes involved by $L_{I}\equiv\{T_{a},B_{a}\}$ , we can construct a convenient basis of integrals by considering the projective simplices involving all possible $n$ -tuples of planes:

$$ [L_{1}\cdots L_{n}]\equiv{\rm d}\log L_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge{\rm d}\log L_{n}\,. $$

Note that this is an $n$ -form in the space of integration variables, $x_{a}$ , and so the exterior derivative in this equation is with respect to these coordinates. This dlog form can be thought of as the canonical form of the (projective) simplex formed from the intersection of $n$ hyperplanes with the plane at infinity $L_{\infty}$ . (For a brief review of the salient features of projective geometry, see Appendix A.) In general, there are far more possible $n$ -tuples of intersecting planes than the dimension of the master integral basis. This is because a typical choice of planes will not bound a finite region. Instead, we must take linear combinations of these projective simplices to obtain bounded regions.1616 16 It may also happen that some of the planes in (4.1) are parallel, in which case the bracket will simply vanish.

To determine the combinations of brackets (4.1) of interest, we introduce the boundary operator

$$ \partial[L_{1}\cdots L_{n}]\equiv\sum_{J=1}^{n}(-1)^{J+1}[L_{1}\cdots\widehat{L}_{J}\cdots L_{n}]\,, $$

where $\penalty\ \,\widehat{}\,\penalty\$ indicates the omission of that hyperplane. We then search for linear combinations that have vanishing boundary. The vector space of cycles with respect to this operation is the space of integrands defining our master integrals.1717 17 In fact, given a hyperplane arrangement, this seems to be one of the more efficient ways to count the number of bounded regions.

#### Two-site chain:

Let us illustrate this procedure for the case of the two-site chain. The relevant hyperplane arrangement was given in Figure 2 and consists of the five lines (3.3):

$$ \displaystyle T_{1} \displaystyle\equiv x_{1}\,,\qquad B_{1}\equiv X_{1}+x_{1}+Y\,, \displaystyle T_{2} \displaystyle\equiv x_{2}\,,\qquad B_{2}\equiv X_{2}+x_{2}+Y\,,\qquad B_{3}\equiv X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}\,. $$

Since the arrangement is not generic, these lines intersect in only 8 places (as opposed to 10 for a generic configuration). We can write a general linear combination as

$$ \Omega=c_{1}[B_{1}B_{2}]+c_{2}[B_{1}B_{3}]+c_{3}[B_{1}T_{2}]+c_{4}[B_{2}B_{3}]+c_{5}[B_{2}T_{1}]+c_{6}[B_{3}T_{1}]+c_{7}[B_{3}T_{2}]+c_{8}[T_{1}T_{2}]\,. $$

There is a four-dimensional space of combinations that are annihilated by $\partial$ , and a convenient choice of basis is

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\psi} \displaystyle=[B_{1}B_{2}]+[B_{2}B_{3}]+[B_{3}B_{1}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{F} \displaystyle=[T_{1}B_{2}]+[B_{2}B_{3}]+[B_{3}T_{1}]=\Omega_{\psi}(B_{1}\to T_{1})\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{F}} \displaystyle=[B_{1}T_{2}]+[T_{2}B_{3}]+[B_{3}B_{1}]=\Omega_{\psi}(B_{2}\to T_{2})\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{Z} \displaystyle=\,[T_{1}T_{2}]+[T_{2}B_{3}]\,+[B_{3}T_{1}]=\Omega_{\psi}(B_{1}\to T_{1},B_{2}\to T_{2})\,. $$

It is straightforward to check that these forms are boundary-less. The simplest way is to note that the flat-space wavefunction can be written as the boundary of a higher-dimensional object

$$ \Omega_{\psi}=\partial[B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}]\,, $$

with similar expressions for the other functions (and recall that $\partial^{2}=0$ ). Notice also that the wavefunction is the unique form that is both annihilated by $\partial$ and which has vanishing residues on $T_{1}=0$ and $T_{2}=0$ . This basis is particularly convenient because $\Omega_{\psi}$ is the form that appears in the integrand of the two-site wavefunction itself, and the other forms are related to $\Omega_{\psi}$ by simple replacements of the boundary lines $B_{1},B_{2}$ with the twisted lines $T_{1},T_{2}$ .

#### Three-site chain:

As a more nontrivial example, we consider the integral associated to the three-site chain (2.28):

$$ \psi_{(3)}=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x_{1}\,{\rm d}x_{2}\,{\rm d}x_{3}\,(x_{1}x_{2}x_{3})^{\varepsilon}\frac{4YY^{\prime}}{B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}B_{4}}\left(\frac{1}{B_{5}}+\frac{1}{B_{6}}\right). $$

Recall that this integral is singular on the following six (untwisted) hyperplanes

$$ \displaystyle B_{1} \displaystyle=X_{1}+x_{1}+Y\,, \displaystyle\qquad B_{4} \displaystyle=X_{1}+X_{2}+X_{3}+x_{1}+x_{2}+x_{3}\,, \displaystyle B_{2} \displaystyle=X_{2}+x_{2}+Y+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{5} \displaystyle=X_{1}+X_{2}+x_{1}+x_{2}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{3} \displaystyle=X_{3}+x_{3}+Y^{\prime}\,, \displaystyle B_{6} \displaystyle=X_{2}+X_{3}+x_{2}+x_{3}+Y\,, $$

along with the three twisted planes $T_{1,2,3}=x_{1,2,3}$ . The arrangement defined by these 9 planes has 25 bounded regions, but already in this example directly visualizing the arrangement to count is challenging.1818 18 Aside from the approach taken in this section, another way to determine the number of bounded regions is to consider these hyperplanes not in $\mathbb{R}^{d}$ , but in some finite field $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}$ , with $p$ being a prime number. This is a discrete lattice of $p^{d}$ points. We then count the number of points not on the hyperplanes. This count $c(p)$ is a polynomial in $p$ of degree $d$ and $|c(1)|$ is the number of bounded regions. To determine $c(p)$ , one counts the number of points which do not vanish mod $p$ for $d+1$ different primes $p$ (for example, by evaluating the product of the $L_{I}$ on all $p^{d}$ points in $\mathbb{F}_{p}^{d}$ ). This fixes the coefficients and we can then evaluate $c(1)=25$ . The intersecting surfaces therefore bound 25 regions. See Appendix A for more details.

There are naively $9$ choose $3$ $=84$ intersections of planes that can be used to form the brackets (4.1). However, the hyperplane arrangement in this example is highly non-generic, because there are linear relations between the functions $B_{a}$ . This means that certain planes don’t intersect. (For example, the linear relation $B_{1}+B_{6}=B_{4}+2Y$ implies that $[B_{1}B_{4}B_{6}]=0$ . Similar relations hold for the set of planes $B_{3},B_{4},B_{5}$ , along with $B_{1},B_{2},B_{5}$ and $B_{2},B_{3},B_{6}$ .) Additionally, there is an interesting four-term relation $B_{2}+B_{4}=B_{5}+B_{6}$ . Taking all of these relations into account, there are $50$ nonzero brackets and a general linear combination of them is

$$ \Omega=\sum c_{IJK}[IJK]\,, $$

where $I,J,K$ run over all the planes. We find a $25$ -dimensional space of forms annihilated by the boundary operator (4.2). The integrand of the wavefunction appearing in (4.7) is the specific linear combination

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\psi}= \displaystyle[B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}]-[B_{1}B_{2}B_{6}]-[B_{1}B_{3}B_{4}]+[B_{1}B_{3}B_{5}]+[B_{1}B_{3}B_{6}] \displaystyle-[B_{1}B_{4}B_{5}]-[B_{2}B_{3}B_{5}]+[B_{2}B_{4}B_{5}]-[B_{2}B_{4}B_{6}]+[B_{3}B_{4}B_{6}]\,. $$

This form is the unique boundary-less object that does not involve any of the twisted planes. We will not choose a specific basis for the other 24 integrals at this stage, since we will shortly be working with a smaller basis tailored to our problem. An interesting feature of the form (4.10) is that it is completely determined by its pattern of vanishing residues, much like the wavefunction integrand for the two-site graph.1919 19 This pattern appears to end here—the four-site chain wavefunction is not uniquely specified by demanding a certain set of zeroes.

It is straightforward to consider more complicated examples following the same procedure. Given the possible singularities of the integrand of interest, we can consider the arrangement cut out by these hyperplanes and search for combinations of intersections of the planes that are annihilated by (4.2). This then serves as a basis for all the possible integrands that can appear when we differentiate the wavefunction. We now consider this second step.

### 4.2 Differential Equations

When we differentiate the wavefunction, we necessarily generate new functions whose integrands involve the twisted planes. These functions can always be decomposed into the basis obtained in the previous step, so the challenge is essentially to figure out what linear combinations of functions appear. This is made quite simple by considering the differential of the individual terms in (4.1). As proven in the box below, the following identity holds inside of a twisted integral

where the total differential ${\rm d}$ is with respect to the kinematic variables $Z_{I}\equiv\{X_{a},Y_{ab}\}$ , and we have defined $L_{a}\equiv\hat{L}_{a}\cdot P$ , where $P^{I}\equiv(1,x_{1},\cdots,x_{n})$ . Note that $\hat{L}_{a,I}$ is the expression for a given hyperplane in projective coordinates. The boundary operation is defined as in (4.2), while the angle bracket is the determinant

$$ \langle\hat{L}_{1}\cdots\hat{L}_{n+1}\rangle\equiv\det(\hat{L}_{1},\cdots,\hat{L}_{n+1})\,. $$

With this formula, we can easily convert derivatives with respect to external kinematics into linear combinations of simplex forms, but now involving the twisted planes.

We emphasize that the simple formula (4.11) is based on the physical properties of the wavefunction and is therefore not applicable to generic simplices. Recall that the hyperplane arrangements associated with the FRW wavefunction are highly non-generic due to the linear relations they satisfy. Notably, these hyperplanes have the property that each coordinate $x_{a}$ always comes in pairs with an external variable $X_{a}$ , allowing us to interchange $\partial_{X_{a}}$ with $\partial_{x_{a}}$ . It is this special characteristic that enables us to easily differentiate projective simplices in the integrands with respect to the external kinematics, and subsequently elevate these to the differentials of the integrated functions.

We can use (4.11) to differentiate each of the terms appearing in the wavefunction. After that, we just have to decompose the result back into whatever basis we choose for the integral family. This linear algebra problem can be solved in many ways, but it is often most convenient to choose a basis where as few elements as possible share singularities and then match residues on these singularities. We now show how this works in some cases.

### 4.3 Selected Examples

Deriving the differential equation for the wavefunction $\psi$ is now completely algorithmic. We first enumerate a basis of canonical forms written in terms of simplices, and then use (4.11) to differentiate each dlog form that appears in the wavefunction. We then introduce new functions as necessary to write the result back in terms of the original wavefunction, plus new pieces. We then differentiate these new pieces and keep going until the system closes. Remarkably, proceeding in this way typically requires fewer functions than occur for totally generic twists.

#### Two-site chain:

We first revisit the example of the two-site chain. In the simplex basis, the canonical form associated to the wavefunction was given in (4.5):

$$ \Omega_{\psi}=[B_{1}B_{2}]+[B_{2}B_{3}]+[B_{3}B_{1}]\,. $$

Using (4.11), we have

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}[B_{1}B_{2}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\Big({\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\,\partial[T_{1}B_{1}B_{2}]+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,\partial[T_{2}B_{1}B_{2}]\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}[B_{2}B_{3}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\Big({\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)\,\partial[T_{1}B_{2}B_{3}]+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,\partial[T_{2}B_{2}B_{3}]\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}[B_{3}B_{1}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\Big({\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\,\partial[T_{1}B_{3}B_{1}]+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\,\partial[T_{2}B_{3}B_{1}]\Big)\,. $$

This means that we can write the total differential of the wavefunction integrand as

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{\psi}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\rm{\displaystyle d}\log(X_{1}+Y)\,\partial\big([T_{1}B_{1}B_{2}]+[T_{1}B_{3}B_{1}]\big)+{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)\,\partial[T_{1}B_{2}B_{3}] \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\rm{\displaystyle d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,\partial\big([T_{2}B_{1}B_{2}]+[T_{2}B_{2}B_{3}]\big)+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\,\partial[T_{2}B_{3}B_{1}]\Big)\,. $$

It is convenient to identify the coefficients of the dlog forms involving the letters $X_{1}-Y$ and $X_{2}-Y$ as the integrands of new functions, which we call $\Omega_{F}$ and $\Omega_{\tilde{F}}$ , respectively. Using $\partial[abc]=[ab]+[bc]+[ca]$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{F} \displaystyle=[T_{1}B_{2}]+[B_{2}B_{3}]+[B_{3}T_{1}]=\Omega_{\psi}(B_{1}\to T_{1})\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{F}} \displaystyle=[B_{1}T_{2}]+[T_{2}B_{3}]+[B_{3}B_{1}]=\Omega_{\psi}(B_{2}\to T_{2})\,. $$

We see that the new forms $\Omega_{F}$ and $\Omega_{\tilde{F}}$ are the ones that we chose as part of our basis in (4.5) with some foresight. They can be obtained from the original form $\Omega_{\psi}$ by replacing boundary lines $B_{a}$ with twisted lines $T_{a}$ . With these definitions, the result in (4.22) can then be written as

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{\psi}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle(\Omega_{\psi}-\Omega_{F})\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+\Omega_{F}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle(\Omega_{\psi}-\Omega_{\tilde{F}})\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)+\Omega_{\tilde{F}}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\Big)\,, $$

where $\Omega_{F}$ and $\Omega_{\tilde{F}}$ appear as sources.

We now repeat the above procedure to obtain the derivatives of these functions. To evaluate ${\rm d}\Omega_{F}$ , we again use (4.11) and write the total differentials of the simplex basis forms as

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}[T_{1}B_{2}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,\partial[T_{2}T_{1}B_{2}]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}[B_{2}B_{3}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\Big({\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)\,\partial[T_{1}B_{2}B_{3}]+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,\partial[T_{2}B_{2}B_{3}]\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}[B_{3}T_{1}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,\partial[T_{2}B_{3}T_{1}]\,, $$

so that the differential of $\Omega_{F}$ is

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{F}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\rm{\displaystyle d}\log(X_{1}-Y)\,\partial[T_{1}B_{2}B_{3}]+{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)\,\partial\big([T_{2}T_{1}B_{2}]+[T_{2}B_{2}B_{3}]\big) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle\rm{\displaystyle d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,\partial[T_{2}B_{3}T_{1}]\Big)\,. $$

As before, it makes sense to call the coefficient of ${\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})$ a new function, as this is the first appearance of this letter. We call this form $\Omega_{Z}$ , and it is easy to see that it is related to $\Omega_{F}$ by the replacement $B_{2}\to T_{2}$ . With this definition, the result (4.26) becomes

$$ {\rm d}\Omega_{F}=\varepsilon\,\Big(\,\Omega_{F}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+(\Omega_{F}-\Omega_{Z})\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)+\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\Big)\,. $$

By symmetry, a similar result holds for $\tilde{F}$ , with $X_{1}\leftrightarrow X_{2}$ and the same function $\Omega_{Z}$ (which can also be obtained from $\Omega_{\tilde{F}}$ by replacing $B_{1}\to T_{1}$ ).

Lastly, we evaluate ${\rm d}\Omega_{Z}$ . Using (4.11) again, we have the differentials

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}[T_{1}T_{2}] \displaystyle=0\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}[T_{2}B_{3}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,\partial[T_{1}T_{2}B_{3}]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}[B_{3}T_{1}] \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,\partial[T_{2}B_{3}T_{1}]\,. $$

In this case, no new functions appear. Instead, we just get back $\Omega_{Z}$ and the system closes:

$$ {\rm d}\Omega_{Z}=2\varepsilon\,\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,. $$

The equations for the actual functions (as opposed to the integrands) are obtained by simply integrating (4.24), (4.27), and (4.29) against the twist factor. This gives

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\psi \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\big[(\psi-F)\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+F\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y) \displaystyle+(\psi-\tilde{F})\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)+\tilde{F}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)\big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}F \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\big[F\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}-Y)+(F-Z)\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}+Y)+Z\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\tilde{F} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\big[\tilde{F}\,{\rm d}\log(X_{2}-Y)+(\tilde{F}-Z)\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+Y)+Z\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}Z \displaystyle=2\varepsilon\,Z\,{\rm d}\log(X_{1}+X_{2})\,, $$

which is precisely the same as (3.26).

The advantage of this approach is that it is completely algorithmic, and does not require us to understand the geometric details of the hyperplane arrangement. Moreover, we are led to a natural basis of functions: as each new letter appears when we take derivatives, we call its coefficient a new function and continue on. This systematic procedure readily generalizes to more complicated examples, as we will now see.

#### Three-site chain:

Above we found that the form associated to the three-site chain is

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\psi}= \displaystyle[B_{1}B_{2}B_{3}]-[B_{1}B_{2}B_{6}]-[B_{1}B_{3}B_{4}]+[B_{1}B_{3}B_{5}]+[B_{1}B_{3}B_{6}] \displaystyle-[B_{1}B_{4}B_{5}]-[B_{2}B_{3}B_{5}]+[B_{2}B_{4}B_{5}]-[B_{2}B_{4}B_{6}]+[B_{3}B_{4}B_{6}]\,. $$

The procedure is now the same as it was for the two-site chain. To evaluate ${\rm d}\Omega_{\psi}$ , we apply (4.11) to each term $[IJK]$ on the right-hand side of (4.31) and identify the coefficients multiplying the resulting “letters” as new functions. We then act with ${\rm d}$ on each of these functions and repeat the procedure until the system closes. for the letters. Taking the total differential of $\Omega_{\psi}$ using (4.11), we get

where the coefficients of the dlog forms are given by the following simplex forms

which allows us to write the remaining coefficient functions in terms of these functions and $\Omega_{\psi}$ :

We then proceed in the same way and take the differential of the source functions. First, consider $\Omega_{F}$ and $\Omega_{\tilde{F}}$ . Taking their differentials gives

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{F}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\Omega_{F}\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{-}+\Omega_{f}\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{-}+(\Omega_{F}-\Omega_{f})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+}+\Omega_{q_{1}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{+} \displaystyle+\Omega_{q_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{-}+\Omega_{q_{3}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{+-}+(\Omega_{F}-\Omega_{q_{1}}-\Omega_{q_{2}}-\Omega_{q_{3}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{++}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{\tilde{F}}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{F}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{-}+\Omega_{f}\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{-}+(\Omega_{\tilde{F}}-\Omega_{f})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{+}+\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{+} \displaystyle+\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{-}+\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{3}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{-+}+(\Omega_{\tilde{F}}-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}}-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}}-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{3}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{++}\Big)\,, $$

where we have expressed the coefficients of the dlog forms in terms of the newly defined sources

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{f} \displaystyle\equiv[245]-[246]+[25\tilde{3}]-[26\tilde{1}]-[2\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]-[45\tilde{1}]+[46\tilde{3}]-[4\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]+[5\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]+[6\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{q_{1}} \displaystyle\equiv[35\tilde{1}]-[35\tilde{2}]+[3\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]-[45\tilde{1}]+[45\tilde{2}]-[4\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{q_{2}} \displaystyle\equiv-[34\tilde{1}]+[34\tilde{2}]-[3\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]+[4\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{q_{3}} \displaystyle\equiv[346]-[34\tilde{2}]+[36\tilde{1}]+[3\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]-[46\tilde{2}]-[6\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]\,, $$

along with

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}} \displaystyle\equiv-[145]+[14\tilde{2}]-[15\tilde{3}]+[1\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]+[45\tilde{2}]-[5\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}} \displaystyle\equiv-[14\tilde{2}]+[14\tilde{3}]-[1\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]+[4\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{3}} \displaystyle\equiv[16\tilde{2}]-[16\tilde{3}]+[1\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]-[46\tilde{2}]+[46\tilde{3}]-[4\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]\,. $$

The equations (4.39) involve four new letters, $X_{12}^{+}$ , $X_{12}^{-}$ , $X_{23}^{+}$ , and $X_{23}^{-}$ , and we have identified their coefficients as new sources, which we call $\Omega_{q_{1}}$ , $\Omega_{q_{2}}$ , $\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}}$ , and $\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}}$ , respectively. Notice that these are exactly the same replacements that were used to obtain the previous sources from $\Omega_{\psi}$ in (4.38). Due to the commutative nature of the replacement operations, these sources with two twisted planes can be obtained via two different paths.

Taking the differential of $\Omega_{Q_{1,2,3}}$ , we find

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{Q_{1}}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\Omega_{Q_{1}}{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{-+}+\Omega_{q_{1}}{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{+}+(\Omega_{Q_{1}}-\Omega_{q_{1}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{+} \displaystyle-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{-}+(\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}}+\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{+}+(\Omega_{Q_{1}}-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{Q_{2}}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\Omega_{Q_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{--}+\Omega_{q_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{-}+(\Omega_{Q_{2}}-\Omega_{q_{2}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{+} \displaystyle+\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{-}+(\Omega_{Q_{2}}-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{Q_{3}}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\Omega_{Q_{3}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{+-}+\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{3}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{+}+(\Omega_{Q_{3}}-\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{3}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+} \displaystyle-\Omega_{q_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{-}+(\Omega_{q_{2}}+\Omega_{q_{3}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{-}+(\Omega_{Q_{3}}-\Omega_{q_{3}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{+}\Big)\,. $$

No new sources are necessary this time, since the source assignments of these equations are completely fixed in terms of the sources already defined.

We now move on to the differential equations for the sources with two twisted planes. First, the differential of $\Omega_{f}$ can be expressed as

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{f}=\varepsilon\,\Big( \displaystyle\Omega_{f}\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{-}+\Omega_{f}\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{-}+\Omega_{g}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{+}+\Omega_{\tilde{g}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{+} \displaystyle+\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log X_{123}+(\Omega_{f}-\Omega_{g}-\Omega_{\tilde{g}}-\Omega_{Z})\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{++}\Big)\,, $$

in terms of three new sources

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{g} \displaystyle\equiv-[45\tilde{1}]+[45\tilde{2}]-[4\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]+[5\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]-[5\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]+[\tilde{1}\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{g}} \displaystyle\equiv-[46\tilde{2}]+[46\tilde{3}]+[4\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]-[6\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]+[6\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]+[\tilde{1}\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{Z} \displaystyle\equiv[4\tilde{1}\tilde{2}]-[4\tilde{1}\tilde{3}]+[4\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]-[\tilde{1}\tilde{2}\tilde{3}]\,. $$

Perhaps unsurprisingly, these can be obtained using the same replacement rules used earlier as

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{g} \displaystyle=\Omega_{q_{1}}(3\to\tilde{3})=\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{3}}(1\to\tilde{1})=\Omega_{f}(2,6\to\tilde{2})-\Omega_{f}(2,5,6\to\tilde{2})\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{\tilde{g}} \displaystyle=\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1}}(3\to\tilde{3})=\Omega_{q_{3}}(1\to\tilde{1})=\Omega_{f}(2,6\to\tilde{2})-\Omega_{f}(2,5,6\to\tilde{2})\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{Z} \displaystyle=\Omega_{q_{2}}(3\to\tilde{3})=\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{2}}(1\to\tilde{1})=\Omega_{f}(2,5,6\to\tilde{2})\,, $$

via three different commuting paths. These sources then fully determine the coefficients appearing in the differentials of $\Omega_{q_{1,2,3}}$ as

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{q_{1}} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\Big(2\Omega_{q_{1}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{+}+(\Omega_{q_{1}}-\Omega_{g})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+}+(\Omega_{g}+\Omega_{Z})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{-}-\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log X_{123}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{q_{2}} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\Big(2\Omega_{q_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{-}+\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log X_{123}+(\Omega_{q_{2}}-\Omega_{Z})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{q_{3}} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\Big(\Omega_{q_{3}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{2}^{+-}-\Omega_{q_{2}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{-}+(\Omega_{q_{3}}+\Omega_{q_{2}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{-} \displaystyle+\Omega_{\tilde{g}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{+}+(\Omega_{q_{3}}-\Omega_{\tilde{g}})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{+}\Big)\,. $$

The differentials of $\Omega_{\tilde{q}_{1,2,3}}$ can be obtained from these by permutation symmetry.

Finally, taking the differential of the sources with three twisted planes gives

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{g} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\Big(2\Omega_{g}\,{\rm d}\log X_{12}^{+}-\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log X_{123}+(\Omega_{g}+\Omega_{Z})\,{\rm d}\log X_{3}^{-}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{\tilde{g}} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\,\Big(2\Omega_{\tilde{g}}\,{\rm d}\log X_{23}^{+}-\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log X_{123}+(\Omega_{\tilde{g}}+\Omega_{Z})\,{\rm d}\log X_{1}^{-}\Big)\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\Omega_{Z} \displaystyle=3\varepsilon\,\Omega_{Z}\,{\rm d}\log X_{123}\,. $$

We see that no additional sources are required this time, and the system therefore closes.

The different colors indicate the four layers of the differential equations or equivalently the number of twisted planes that define the functions. The components of the matrix can be read off from the equations (4.33), (4.39), (4.43), (4.47), and (4.48), or the Mathematica notebook available at . It can be checked that this matrix indeed satisfies the integrability condition $\tilde{A}\wedge\tilde{A}=0$ .

Some reordering of the functions is needed to put the matrix in a manifestly triangular form, due to the mixing between functions within the same layer. For instance, $q_{2}$ (or $\tilde{q}_{2}$ ) appears as a source in the equation for $q_{3}$ (or $\tilde{q}_{3}$ ), while $Z$ appears as a source in the equations for both $g$ and $\tilde{g}$ . Relatedly, taking the de Sitter limit $\varepsilon\to 0$ no longer amounts to simply deleting the diagonal entries as in the two-site case, since the rescaling in $\varepsilon$ depends on the number of twisted planes.

As in the two-site case, we can solve the differential equations line-by-line and obtain the physical solution for $\psi$ after imposing the correct boundary conditions. We provide the details of this procedure in Appendix D. For $\varepsilon=0$ , the solution is given in terms of classical polylogarithms up to transcendental weight three [7]. Moreover, it can be checked that the above matrix in the $\varepsilon\to 0$ limit correctly reproduces the symbol of the de Sitter wavefunction (see Appendix E for details). For negative integer $\varepsilon$ , which includes the flat-space case $\varepsilon=-1$ , the solution is given by a rational function. For generic $\varepsilon$ , the solution is given by an integral over a ${}_{2}F_{1}$ , which gives a two-variable generalization of the hypergeometric series.

### 4.4 Source Functions

The previous examples suggest that all sources in the differential equations may be obtained through suitable “replacement rules” starting from the wavefunction integrand and replacing untwisted planes $B_{a}$ by twisted ones $T_{a}$ . It turns out that this is indeed the case, and this gives a systematic way to generate all source functions for any tree graph.

For the two-site chain, there were two replacement rules, one for each vertex:

$$ \displaystyle 1 \displaystyle:\quad F=\psi(B_{1}\to T_{1})\,,\quad Z=\tilde{F}(B_{1}\to T_{1})\,, \displaystyle 2 \displaystyle:\quad\tilde{F}=\psi(B_{2}\to T_{2})\,,\quad Z=F(B_{2}\to T_{2})\,. $$

Note that the functions $F$ and $\tilde{F}$ in (4.30) were associated to the letters $X_{1}-Y$ and $X_{2}-Y$ with flipped signs of the internal energies. These correspond to folded singularities that are not present in the Bunch–Davies wavefunction, whose physical energy singularities were represented by various tubings of a graph, cf. (2.14) and (2.15). It turns out that there is a simple graphical way to capture the dependence on folded singularities with a slight modification of the previous tubing picture, in terms of a “marked graph”. In this dressed version of a graph, we add a cross for every edge of a graph as an extra label for internal energies, and the nodes indicate external energies as usual. Folded singularities are then indicated by tubings that enclose these crosses. This modified tubing picture is necessary to capture all singularities and basis functions that are present in the differential equations before imposing boundary conditions. The relation between the parent function $\psi$ and its source functions can then be graphically depicted as

$$ \psi F 1 2 2 1 \tilde{F} Z $$

Here, each source function is associated to a tubing of a marked graph, containing at least one cross (except the wavefunction, which corresponds to a graph without any tubings). Each substitution of a twisted plane $T_{i}$ is represented by a tube enclosing the vertex $i$ . When the two tubings corresponding to $F$ and $\tilde{F}$ overlap, i.e. when they share a cross, their union is represented by a merged tubing. This new tubing is associated to the function $Z$ .

For the three-site chain, the source functions were obtained from $\psi$ using five different replacement rules: one for each of the end vertices $X_{1}$ and $X_{3}$ , and three for the middle vertex $X_{2}$ . In the equation for the wavefunction, these were

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}1&:\quad F=\psi(B_{1}\to T_{1})\,,\\
2_{1}&:\ \ \,Q_{1}=\psi(B_{2,6}\to T_{2})-\psi(B_{2,5,6}\to T_{2})\,,\\
2_{2}&:\ \ \,Q_{2}=\psi(B_{2,5,6}\to T_{2})\,,\\
2_{3}&:\ \ \,Q_{3}=\psi(B_{2,5}\to T_{2})-\psi(B_{2,5,6}\to T_{2})\,,\\
3&:\quad\tilde{F}=\psi(B_{3}\to T_{3})\,,\end{split} $$

where $i_{r}$ refers to the $r$ -th replacement operation for vertex $i$ (so that e.g. $2_{2}$ is the second replacement rule for vertex $2$ ). In the differential equation, these source functions were associated with new letters involving at least one sign flip of the internal energies for lines a vertex is connected to. The number of replacement rules for each vertex is therefore given by $2^{e-1}$ for a vertex connected to $e$ edges. As in the two-site case, the relations between $\psi$ and its source functions can be graphically represented as

$$ \psi F 1 Q_{1} Q_{2} 2_{1} 2_{2} 2_{3} Q_{3} \tilde{F} 3 q_{1} q_{2} q_{3} \tilde{q}_{3} \tilde{q}_{2} \tilde{q}_{1} f Z \tilde{g} g $$

We see that there are a total of 16 basis functions in the differential system including $\psi$ itself.

This graphical representation of basis functions can be straightforwardly generalized to arbitrary tree graphs. Since the substituted twisted planes do not need to be adjacent to each other, they can be depicted as a union of disconnected tubings of a marked graph. There are four independent tubings for a graph with one edge (i.e. the two-site chain), and a simple inductive argument implies that the total number of independent tubings for a graph with $e$ edges is $4^{e}$ , irrespective of its geometry.2020 20 This counting is also given by the normalized volume of cosmological polytopes [93, 94]. This establishes a one-to-one correspondence between the basis functions in the differential equations and the disconnected tubings of a marked graph. The basis functions are therefore elegantly characterized by the combinatorics of a marked graph, a topic that will be explored in greater detail in the next section.

#### Function count:

We can also easily count the number of basis functions in different layers, where a layer refers to the number of vertices enclosed in the tubings (or, equivalently, the number of substituted twisted planes). For a graph $G$ , the number of disconnected tubings $t_{\ell}$ at layer $\ell$ is

$$ t_{\ell}(G)=\sum_{x_{1}+\cdots+x_{r_{\rm max}}=\ell}\ \prod_{r=1}^{r_{\rm max}}\binom{a_{r}}{x_{r}}(2^{r}-1)^{x_{r}}\,, $$

where $r=1,2,\cdots,r_{\rm max}$ is the number of neighboring edges for a vertex, $a_{r}$ is the number of vertices of $G$ having exactly $r$ edges, and $x_{r}$ is the number of vertices enclosed in tubings that have exactly $r$ edges for a given layer. Interestingly, the alternating sum of the number of functions in each layer always vanishes, regardless of its geometry:

$$ \displaystyle\sum_{\ell}(-1)^{\ell}\,t_{\ell}=0\,. $$

This feature holds in general and suggests the existence of some underlying geometric object.

Let us give a few examples. For the $n$ -site chain, we have $r_{\rm max}=2$ , with $a_{1}=2$ and $a_{2}=n-2$ . The number of functions in the $\ell$ -th layer of the differential equation then is

$$ \displaystyle t_{\ell}(\text{$n$-site chain})=\binom{n-2}{\ell}\,3^{\ell}+2\binom{n-2}{\ell-1}\,3^{\ell-1}+\binom{n-2}{\ell-2}\,3^{\ell-2}\,. $$

Explicitly, this gives $\{t_{0},t_{1},t_{2}\}=\{1,2,1\}$ for the two-site chain, $\{t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},t_{3}\}=\{1,5,7,3\}$ for the three-site chain as we have found above, and $\{t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\}=\{1,8,22,24,9\}$ for the four-site chain. For a pure star geometry, we have $a_{1}=n-1$ , $a_{n-1}=1$ and $a_{i}=0$ , for $i\notin\{1,n-1\}$ . This gives

$$ \displaystyle t_{\ell}(\text{$n$-site star})=\binom{n-1}{\ell}+\binom{n-1}{\ell-1}(2^{n-1}-1)\,. $$

The simplest graph with a star geometry is the four-site star, which has $\{t_{0},t_{1},t_{2},t_{3},t_{4}\}=\{1,10,24,22,7\}$ .

Note that this is similar to how the functions $Q_{1,2,3}$ were obtained in the three-site case, involving a subtraction of the function involving both crosses enclosed in the tubing. A new feature is that the replacement $2_{2}$ involves two planes $B_{7}$ and $B_{10}$ that contain both $X_{2}$ and $X_{3}$ , with $B_{10}$ also containing $X_{4}$ . The source functions for vertex 3 can be obtained in a similar way.

A slightly more nontrivial example is the four-site star, whose wavefunction integrand and boundary planes were given in (2.33) and (2.34).
